This is a **microscopic image** showing fungal spores/conidia. Key features:
- Multicellular, septate spores with transverse and longitudinal septa
- Club/hand-grenade shaped conidia
- Formed in chains (visible in center)
- Light olive-brown coloration

This strongly matches Alternaria conidia. The KB description for Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers states: "Spores are formed in chains of 3-5, light olive brown to dark brown, hand grenade-shaped with a shorter beaked apical cell."

Let me verify by viewing reference images across 8 classes as required.
None of these macro references match the microscopic test image. Let me continue viewing references from 4 more classes to fulfill the 8-class requirement.

All 8 references viewed. Key comparisons:

- **Late_Blight** (Bugwood_10.jpg) is also microscopic, showing lemon-shaped, single-celled sporangia on branching sporangiophores. Very different from the test image's multicellular, septate conidia.
- **Rhizopus_Soft_Rots** (Bugwood_2.jpg) shows tangled whitish mycelia with round black sporangia. Also very different.
- The remaining references (Anthracnose, Early Blight, Gray Mold, Septoria, Sclerotinia, Alternaria stem image) are all macro-level plant symptom photos, none microscopic.

**Analysis of the test image spore morphology:**
- Multicellular conidia with both **transverse and longitudinal septa** (muriform)
- **Club/hand-grenade shape** with a narrower beak at one end
- Formed in **chains** (clearly visible in the center of the image)
- **Light olive-brown** coloration
- Size consistent with ~18-50 µm range

This matches the KB description for Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers exactly: *"Spores are formed in chains of 3-5, light olive brown to dark brown, hand grenade-shaped with a shorter beaked apical cell on the terminal end, and are 7-18 x 18-50 µm in size."*

No other class in this dataset produces conidia with this morphology.

This perfectly matches the Alternaria KB description of spores formed in chains of 3-5, hand grenade-shaped, 7-18 x 18-50 µm. No other class produces conidia with this distinctive morphology."}
